subChunks.title: Internationalisation (i18n) with react-i18next
subChunks.hookHtml: Internationalisation is not just translating strings — it's handling date and number formats, pluralisation rules that differ by language, right-to-left text direction, locale-aware sorting, and dynamic content that changes structure between languages. react-i18next is the production standard for React i18n, used by companies serving global audiences.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Setup

// i18n.ts:
import i18n from 'i18next';
import { initReactI18next } from 'react-i18next';
import LanguageDetector from 'i18next-browser-languagedetector';
import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend';

i18n
  .use(Backend)           // Load translations from /public/locales
  .use(LanguageDetector)  // Detect browser language
  .use(initReactI18next)
  .init({
    fallbackLng: 'en',
    ns: ['common', 'quests', 'members'],  // Translation namespaces
    defaultNS: 'common',
    interpolation: { escapeValue: false }, // React already escapes
  });

// Translation files:
// public/locales/en/common.json
// public/locales/en/quests.json
// public/locales/fr/common.json

Basic usage

// public/locales/en/quests.json:
{
  "title": "Quest Board",
  "accept": "Accept Quest",
  "questCount": "{{count}} quest",
  "questCount_plural": "{{count}} quests",
  "xpReward": "Reward: {{amount, number}} XP",
  "completedAt": "Completed {{date, datetime}}"
}

// Component:
import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';

function QuestBoard({ questCount, reward, completedAt }) {
  const { t, i18n } = useTranslation('quests');

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{t('title')}</h1>
      {/* Pluralisation — i18next picks _plural when count !== 1: */}
      <p>{t('questCount', { count: questCount })}</p>
      {/* Number formatting per locale: */}
      <p>{t('xpReward', { amount: reward })}</p>
      {/* Date formatting per locale: */}
      <p>{t('completedAt', { date: completedAt })}</p>
    </div>
  );
}

Language switching

function LanguageSelector() {
  const { i18n } = useTranslation();

  return (
    <select
      value={i18n.language}
      onChange={e => i18n.changeLanguage(e.target.value)}
      aria-label="Select language"
    >
      <option value="en">English</option>
      <option value="fr">Français</option>
      <option value="ar">العربية</option>
    </select>
  );
}

Right-to-left (RTL) support

// Detect RTL languages and set document direction:
const rtlLanguages = ['ar', 'he', 'fa', 'ur'];

function App() {
  const { i18n } = useTranslation();
  const isRtl = rtlLanguages.includes(i18n.language);

  useEffect(() => {
    document.documentElement.dir = isRtl ? 'rtl' : 'ltr';
    document.documentElement.lang = i18n.language;
  }, [isRtl, i18n.language]);

  return <RouterProvider router={router} />;
}

Trans component for JSX in translations

// When the translation contains markup:
// en.json: { "clickHere": "Click <1>here</1> to view your quests" }
import { Trans } from 'react-i18next';

<Trans i18nKey="clickHere">
  Click <Link to="/quests">here</Link> to view your quests
</Trans>

Vex: "The most common i18n mistake: hardcoding sentence structure in JSX. 'You have ' + count + ' quests' assumes English grammar. In German, the number comes at the end. In Russian, pluralisation has 3 forms. Treat the entire sentence as a translation unit — never concatenate strings from separate keys."

storyBeats.text: The guild expands to 40 countries. 'Accept Quest' in English. 'Accepter la Quête' in French. 'قبول المهمة' in Arabic — right to left. '1 quest' becomes '2 quests' but pluralisation has 6 forms in Russian. Vex opens the i18n docs.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Internationalisation is not substituting words. French translates 'Accept Quest' differently depending on the subject's gender. Arabic reads right-to-left. Russian has plural forms for 1, 2-4, 5-20, and other. i18next handles all of this — but you have to give it complete sentence units, not string fragments.

storyBeats.speaker: Never concatenate — always translate complete sentences

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Set up a basic i18n system:

  • Create English and French translation files for quests namespace
  • Build a <QuestBoard /> that uses useTranslation to translate: title, a pluralised quest count, and an XP reward with number formatting
  • Build a <LanguageSelector /> that switches between en/fr
  • Verify the quest count pluralises correctly (1 quest vs 2 quests in English; 1 quête vs 2 quêtes in French)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a fully internationalised quest form with react-i18next (real library, not mock): three languages (English, French, Arabic), pluralisation for quest counts, number formatting for XP (1,500 XP in English vs 1 500 XP in French vs ١٬٥٠٠ نقطة خبرة in Arabic), date formatting, RTL support when Arabic is selected (document.dir = 'rtl'), and the Trans component for a sentence with a link inside it. Use the i18next-browser-languagedetector to default to the browser's language.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why i18n is harder than just translating strings. Give three concrete examples of language-specific behaviour that string substitution can't handle. Walk through the pluralisation system in i18next — how does it pick the right form? Explain the Trans component — what problem does it solve that t() can't?

questions.prompt: You have the string `'You have ' + count + ' quests in ' + category + ' category'`. Why is this problematic for i18n?
options: Sentence structure varies by language — word order, grammatical agreement, and pluralisation rules differ. The entire sentence must be a single translation unit with parameters.
The + operator doesn't work with translated strings
count and category must be translated separately first
It will work fine — i18next handles string concatenation automatically
questions.answer: Sentence structure varies by language — word order, grammatical agreement, and pluralisation rules differ. The entire sentence must be a single translation unit with parameters.
questions.explanation: In German, the verb typically comes at the end: 'Sie haben 3 Quests in der Kampf Kategorie'. In Japanese, the category precedes quests. In Russian, the noun form changes based on count. Concatenating fragments forces all languages into English sentence structure. The solution: t('questSummary', { count, category }) with a complete translated template per language.

questions.prompt: When should you use the `Trans` component instead of `t()`?
options: When the translated text contains interactive or styled elements (links, bold text, buttons) that must be rendered as React components
When the translation key is longer than 20 characters
questions.answer: When the translated text contains interactive or styled elements (links, bold text, buttons) that must be rendered as React components
questions.explanation: t() returns a string — you can't embed a <Link> component in a string. Trans lets you write JSX with numbered slots that the translator can reference: { "clickHere": "Click <1>here</1>" } where <1> maps to your Link component. This lets translators move the link to the right position in their language without the developer hardcoding the position.
